To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

LPA promotes amyloid fibril assembly of beta(2)microglobulin under physiological conditions through the formation of an intermediate conformation, and the fibril formation is accompanied by a structural change of the fibrils.

lysophospholidic acid (a lysophospholpid mediator) destabilizes the structure and increases the conformational flexibility of beta2-microglobulin, a major component of amyloid fibrils, which leads to its aggregation and amyloid fibril deposition.

lysophospholidic acid (a lipid mediator occurring in vivo) promotes amyloid formation of beta(,2)-microglobuline (a protein involved in dialysis-related amiloidosis) under physiological conditions through an intricate mechanism, and that the molecular organization and stability of fibrils formed in the presence of lysophospholatic acid differ from that of fibril formed at pH 1.5.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the molecular mechanism of amyloid formation and stabilization of beta2m in the presence of the physiological mediator LPA, which is of great relevance for the understanding of the pathomechanisms of beta2m-based fibril deposition in dialysis-related and other amyloid diseases.
a novel molecular mechanism of amyloid formation, in which LPA acts as a conformational switcher of beta2m, and with the molecular mechanism of fibril stabilization by LPA.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanism of amyloid formation of beta2m under physiological conditions, which may help to design novel therapeutic approaches to this disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

lysophospholidic acid (a) induces the formation of amyloid fibrils of beta2m under physiological conditions (b) stabilizes the fibrillar form of beta2m, (c) increases the flexibility of monomeric and fibrillar beta2m and (d) induces the formation and stabilization of fibrils with a distinct molecular organization.
LPA is an in vivo occurring molecule, which is involved in the amyloidogenic process of beta2m.

lysophospholidic acid (a) induces the conformational transition of monomeric b2m into a partially unfolded form; (b) increases the conformational flexibility of b2m; (c) promotes amyloid formation in a nucleation independent manner; (d) stabilizes amyloid fibrils; (e) is a specific b2m binding ligand.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LPA is an amyloidogenic factor for beta2m in the presence of its critical micelle concentrations, and that LPA is a fibril-stabilizer for beta2m below the critical micelle concentrations.
LPA is a physiological mediator of beta2m fibril formation.
LPA is a key factor in the amyloidogenesis of beta2m in dialysis-related and other forms of amyloidosis, and it is the first example that a lysophospholipoprotein mediates amyloid formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of LIPs in the blood of dialysis patients may be a risk factor for the development of beta2m amyloidosis.
LPA can induce the conformational changes in beta(2)- microglobulin (beta2m) necessary for amyloid fibril assembly under physiological conditions, and that LPA stabilizes beta2m fibrils.
lysophospholiphids, which are present in the blood of dialysis patients at elevated levels, can induce amyloid fibril growth of beta2m in vitro under physiological (pH 7) conditions.
